posts.title: Says they can, did it in a test, does it at home
posts.insight: What a person says they can do, what they manage in a test and what they actually do at home are three different measurements. US data show discordance between the first and the last, so a function score should say which one it records.
posts.angle: Anchor measurement in the discharge decision: a score in a letter or a trial report rests on one of three kinds of function, and the reader needs to know which.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical findings (Glass 1998, qualitative description of discordance with no numbers; Bandeen-Roche 2023, moderate agreement) and clinical judgement (state which kind of function a score records), marked as judgement. The WHO ICF claim was not verified and is not used.

captions.x:
"Can you make a hot drink?" has three possible answers: what the person says they can do, what they manage in a test, and what they actually do at home.

A 1998 paper called these three "tenses" of function. In US data from the MacArthur Studies of Successful Aging, what people said they could do and what they did at home showed "a consistent pattern of discordance", meaning the two did not match. The abstract gives no numbers.

In a US study of 5,888 older adults, self-reported difficulty with walking and strength agreed only moderately with measured tests, and one could not simply stand in for the other.

When a function score goes into a discharge letter or a trial report, we should say which of the three it records.
captions.linkedin:
"Can you make a hot drink?" has three possible answers: what the person says they can do, what they manage in a test, and what they actually do at home on an ordinary day.

A 1998 paper in The Gerontologist called these three "tenses" of function: hypothetical (what people say they can do), experimental (what they do in a test) and enacted (what they do at home). It used data from the MacArthur Studies of Successful Aging in the US. These showed "a consistent pattern of discordance" between what people said they could do and what they actually did at home, meaning the two did not match. The abstract gives no numbers, so the size of the gap is not quoted here.

A later US study of 5,888 older adults (Cardiovascular Health Study, 1989 to 1990) found that self-reported difficulty with walking and strength agreed only moderately with measured tests, with agreement scores (kappa) of 0.55 to 0.60, where 1.00 would be perfect agreement. The authors say commonly used self-reported disability items should not be assumed to stand in for the walking and grip tests used to define frailty.

A score that goes into a discharge decision, a care package or a trial outcome records one of the three. Which one it records is a question to ask before relying on it. Asking about an ordinary morning at home is still asking what the person says. Watching what they do at home is a different measurement.

That is a judgement about good practice. We should state in the discharge letter or the trial report which kind of function a score records, and add what the person does day to day.
captions.bluesky: "Can you make a hot drink?" has three answers: what the person says, what they manage in a test, what they do at home. In US data, what people said they could do consistently differed from what they did at home. A function score should say which of the three it records.

"Can you make a hot drink?" has three answers: what the person says, what they manage in a test, and what they do at home.

In US data, what people said they could do consistently differed from what they did at home. In a study of 5,888 older adults, self-reported walking and strength difficulty agreed only moderately with measured tests (agreement scores of 0.55 to 0.60, where 1.00 would be perfect).

A function score should say which of the three it records.

posts.title: Talking therapy in later life
posts.insight: In NHS talking therapy services in London, about 53 in 100 people aged 65 or over recovered, against about 41 in 100 working-age adults, and fewer older people dropped out. Older people made up fewer than 4 in 100 of those treated.
posts.angle: Low mood and worry in later life are treatable. Older people did at least as well in these services, yet few reached them. Give crude figures, state the observational limits, and carry the depression-alone qualification.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical finding (Saunders 2021, observational, London services, selection bias possible) and ethical judgement (older people should be offered talking therapy on the same terms as younger adults), marked as judgement.

captions.x:
Adults aged 65 or over were more likely to recover in NHS talking therapy services in London than working-age adults. Talking therapy means a course of sessions with a trained worker.

The study used service records for 100,179 people treated for depression or anxiety. By the end of treatment, about 53 in 100 older adults had recovered, as the services measured it. For adults aged 18 to 64, it was about 41 in 100. Fewer older people dropped out: 18 in 100, against 32 in 100.

These figures are not adjusted, and older people started with milder symptoms. After allowing for that, older adults were still more likely to recover, but the gap was smaller. This post does not give a figure for the smaller gap. Older people who reach these services may differ from older people who never do.

The gap was larger for anxiety. For depression alone, older adults were still more likely to recover after allowing for how unwell people were at the start. The gap was no longer clear when each older person was compared with working-age adults who were similar in other ways.

Older people were few among those treated: fewer than 4 in 100 were 65 or over, although about 18 in 100 of the population are that age, a figure the authors cite. That comparison is rough.

If you are over 65 and feeling low or anxious, ask your GP about talking therapy.
captions.linkedin:
Adults aged 65 or over were more likely to recover in NHS talking therapy services in London than working-age adults. Talking therapy means a course of sessions with a trained worker, which can include guided self-help.

The study covered 100,179 people treated for depression or anxiety in eight London services between 2008 and 2019. At the end of treatment, about 53 in 100 of those aged 65 or over had recovered, as the services measured it. For those aged 18 to 64, it was about 41 in 100. Fewer older people dropped out: 18 in 100, against 32 in 100.

There are limits to these figures. The study looked at routine service records and did not assign people to treatments. The 53 and 41 in 100 are not adjusted, and older people started with milder symptoms. After allowing for how unwell people were at the start, older adults were still more likely to recover, but the gap was smaller. This post does not give a figure for the smaller gap.

Older people who reach these services may differ from older people who never do, and some differences between the groups may remain. The gap was larger for anxiety. For depression alone, older adults were still more likely to recover after allowing for how unwell people were at the start. The gap was no longer clear when each older person was compared with working-age adults who were similar in other ways. The data come from London services only.

Older people were also few among those treated. Fewer than 4 in 100 people treated in these services were 65 or over, although about 18 in 100 of the population are that age, a background figure the authors cite. That comparison is rough, because need as well as population share counts.

We should treat depression and anxiety in later life as treatable, and offer older people talking therapy on the same terms as younger adults. That is a judgement about fair access.

If you are over 65 and feeling low or anxious, you can ask your GP about talking therapy.

posts.title: Exclusion should need a reason
posts.insight: Adults who lack capacity to consent are often left out of research although the law in England and Wales already allows their inclusion with safeguards. Few protocols give a reason for excluding them.
posts.angle: Reverse the default: studies of conditions common in later life should include adults who lack capacity unless the protocol gives a scientific reason. Stays on default exclusion of people who cannot consent; no trial-population points from other posts.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical findings (Taylor 2012 review; Shepherd 2019 registry review; Shepherd 2024 framework; England and Wales legal route) and ethical judgement (include unless a scientific reason is given), marked as judgement.

captions.x:
Of about 80 UK trials completed in 2015 to 2018 in conditions where impaired capacity is common, 15 allowed adults who lacked capacity to consent to take part. The search was not comprehensive.

In the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society in 2008 and 2009, at least 127 of 434 studies (29%) explicitly excluded people with cognitive impairment, and very few gave any justification.

The law in England and Wales already allows inclusion: drug trials with a legal representative's consent, other research with the advice of a consultee (someone who knows the person and says what they would want).

Judgement: unless the protocol gives a scientific reason, studies of conditions common in later life should include adults who lack capacity, with those safeguards. Exclusion without a stated reason is unfair to them.
captions.linkedin:
Many studies leave out people with cognitive impairment or adults who lack capacity to consent for themselves. Figures from two different settings show how often, and the law is the third point.

1. In a review of 434 original studies in one leading geriatrics journal over two years (2008 and 2009), at least 127 (29%) explicitly excluded people with cognitive impairment. Very few gave any justification.
2. Among about 80 UK trials completed between 2015 and 2018 in conditions where impaired capacity is common, 15 allowed adults who lacked capacity to take part. That search of a trial registry was not comprehensive.
3. In England and Wales, the law already allows inclusion. Drug trials follow the Clinical Trials Regulations 2004, with a legal representative's consent. Other research follows the Mental Capacity Act 2005, with the advice of a consultee (someone who knows the person and says what they would want).

The authors of a UK framework paper say adults with impaired capacity are frequently excluded, partly because researchers are unfamiliar with the legal and ethical frameworks. The UK INCLUDE framework for trials with people who lack capacity to consent gives trial teams four key questions and worksheets for designing trials that include them. Its effect on inclusion has not yet been evaluated.

This is a judgement, not a finding: we should include adults who lack capacity in studies of conditions common in later life, with the legal safeguards, unless the protocol gives a scientific reason not to. Exclusion without a stated reason is unfair to them, and it leaves their care with less evidence.

When you review a protocol, ask whether each exclusion is justified in writing.

Judgement: we should include these adults unless the protocol gives a scientific reason not to.

posts.title: Long-term conditions arrive earlier in deprived areas
posts.insight: In a study of 1.75 million people in Scotland, having two or more long-term conditions became common 10 to 15 years earlier in the most deprived areas than in the most affluent. As an implication, a fixed starting age for a service or study may reach people in deprived areas later in the course of their conditions.
posts.angle: An age threshold looks neutral. Revised angle: built on Barnett 2012 alone (population level, 2007 data), no healthy life expectancy figures, no named age-gated policy; need-based entry offered as judgement.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical finding (Barnett 2012, cross-sectional, population level), interpretation (what a fixed starting age implies, marked as an implication) and ethical judgement (do not rely on age alone as the way in), marked as judgement.

captions.x:
Two or more long-term conditions became common at ages 10 to 15 years younger in the most deprived areas of Scotland than in the most affluent. That comes from a cross-sectional study of 1.75 million people registered with 314 Scottish general practices in March 2007. It compares age groups at one point in time rather than following people.

It describes whole populations, so each person's course will differ. In the same study, slightly more people with two or more long-term conditions were under 65 (210,500) than 65 or over (194,996). The proportion was highest in older people.

This implies that a service or study that opens at a fixed age may reach people in deprived areas later in the course of their conditions.

Judgement: services and studies for older people should not rely on age alone to decide who is eligible. Eligibility based on need, such as help required with everyday tasks, fits the aim better.
captions.linkedin:
Two or more long-term conditions became common at ages 10 to 15 years younger in the most deprived areas of Scotland than in the most affluent.

That comes from a study of 1,751,841 people registered with 314 Scottish general practices, using data from March 2007. It describes whole populations, so each person's course will differ. It is cross-sectional, so it compares age groups at one point in time.

The same study found that slightly more people with two or more long-term conditions were under 65 (210,500) than 65 or over (194,996), although the proportion was highest in older people.

One implication is offered here as interpretation. A service or study that opens at a fixed age may reach people in the most deprived areas later in the course of their conditions. At the same age, people in deprived areas may be further into their conditions.

This is a judgement: services and studies for older people should not rely on age alone to decide who is eligible. If the aim is to reach people who need them, eligibility based on need fits better. It would also give more attention to people who are poorly served. Need could mean, for example, how much help a person needs with everyday tasks.

When you see an age threshold on a service or a study, ask whom it reaches late.

Age alone should not decide who can use services and studies. Need, such as help with everyday tasks, fits better.

posts.title: Several conditions, and health rated good
posts.insight: In a Newcastle study of 85-year-olds, the typical woman had 5 chronic diseases from a list of 18 counted by the researchers and the typical man 4, yet about 3 in 4 rated their health as good, very good or excellent compared with others their age.
posts.angle: The problem list is what services count; self-rated health is what people report. Keep the comparison literal: 5 and 4 diagnoses, 78 in 100 rating good or better, with the 'compared with others their age' wording and the optimism caveat.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Newcastle 85+ baseline, cross-sectional) with a practical suggestion to ask the person; the suggestion is advice, not a finding.

captions.x:
In a Newcastle study, the typical 85-year-old woman had 5 chronic diseases from a list of 18 that the researchers counted, and the typical man had 4. The counts drew on GP records and some tests done at a health assessment, for the 729 people with complete data.

Of the 832 who answered the rating question, about 3 in 4 (646) rated their health as good, very good or excellent compared with others their age.

The most common recorded conditions were high blood pressure (over half of people) and osteoarthritis (about half). About 6 in 10 had hearing loss on assessment.

A disease count reflects what was recorded and tested. A rating records how the person sees their own health. The authors point to a study that combined the results of many studies, which found that in people aged 75 or more, comparing yourself with others your age gives more optimistic ratings.

If an older relative has a long list of conditions, you can ask how they would rate their own health.
captions.linkedin:
The typical 85-year-old woman in a Newcastle study had 5 chronic diseases from a list of 18 that the researchers counted, and the typical man had 4. The counts drew on GP records and some tests done at a health assessment, for the 729 people with complete data.

About 3 in 4 people rated their health as good, very good or excellent compared with others their age. That was 646 of the 832 who answered.

The Newcastle 85+ Study recruited people born in 1921 who were registered with GPs in Newcastle and North Tyneside, including people living in care homes. The most common recorded conditions were high blood pressure (over half of people) and osteoarthritis (about half). About 6 in 10 had hearing loss on assessment.

A disease count reflects what was recorded and tested. A self-rating records how a person sees their own health. There are two cautions. The question asked people to compare themselves with others of the same age, and answers of that kind may be more optimistic. And this study looked at one point in time. It did not follow people over the years.

A long problem list does not tell you how a person rates their own health. If you are a relative, a carer or a clinician, you can ask the person how they would rate their own health, and listen to the answer before assuming.
